latin.1671: XIII. Ut autem distinctius intelligatur quae sit de hac quaestione Doctorum Scholae Romanae sententia, visum est hic referre quae ea de re accurate & perspicue admodum tradit Gul. Estius in secundum sententiarum Distinctione 19. num. 9. Ibi enim ad quaestionem, Utrum immortalitas primi status fuerit homini naturalis, per multas & varias distinctiones Respondet. Et docet eam illi quadam ratione naturalem, & quadam ratione supra naturam fuisse; sicut & mors homini lapso quadam ratione naturalis est, quadam ratione contra naturam.
latin.1672: XIV. Primo enim naturale dicitur quod inest a prima institutione naturae. Et hac ratione dicit immortalitatem fuisse primo homini naturalem, mortem vero contra naturam, quoniam homo initio institutus est immortalis, id est, a moriendi necessitate liber.
latin.1673: XV. Item naturale dicitur id in quod naturaliter fertur cujusque appetitus. Et etiam sic concedit immortalitatem homini naturalem esse, & mortem contra naturam, quoniam omnes natura appetunt immortalitatem, mortem vero refugiunt.
latin.1674: XVI. Praeterea naturale significare potest quod cuique inest a nativitate, sive sit naturae bonum atque conveniens, & naturali appetitui consentaneum, sive non. Et ita quoque fatetur primo homini immortalitatem, mortalitatem vero nobis naturalem esse. Ille enim immortalis conditus fuit, nos autem nascimur morti obnoxii.
latin.1675: XVII. Rursum addit naturale dici id quod in ipsa natura causam habet. Et etiam, inquit, hoc pacto immortalitas fuit primo homini quodammodo naturalis. Nam in optima humani corporis temperie tanquam interna causa, & in ligno vitae tanquam externa causa (quarum utraque ad illum effectum naturalis erat) immortalitas consistebat.
latin.1676: XVIII. Caeterum docet alia ratione eandem immortalitatem homini fuisse supernaturalem: partim quidem ratione justitiae, a qua bona illa corporis constitutio, & ex consequenti immortalitas ipsa dependebat. Erat enim, inquit, illa justitia supernaturalis, quatenus per eam anima Deo subjiciebatur, & adhaerebat, ut bono ac fini suo supernaturali. Qua subjectione durante, inerat animae vis quaedam supernaturalis, per quam poterat corpus, ab omni corruptione praeservare. Partim ratione corporis, sive materiae ex qua homo factus est. Quae cum terrena fuerit, causam in se immortalitatis non habebat, sed potius mortalitatis. Quamvis igitur, inquit, primus homo in ipsa natura causam quandam habuerit immortalitatis, non tamen plenam & totalem. Quin potius si dona supernaturalia cogitatione ab eo separemus, & sola in eo consideremus naturalia, mortalis erat, ita ut necesse esset eum mori. Erat enim compositus ex contrariis, quorum pugnam necessario tandem consequitur ipsius compositi corruptio. Juxta hunc igitur modum immortalitas erat primo homini supernaturalis. Quoniam autem supernaturale proprie non opponitur ei quod primo, secundo, vel tertio modo naturale dicitur ex modis jam enumeratis, sed ei tantum quod quarto modo: secundum quem tamen non potest immortalitas primo homini dici simpliciter naturalis; quia ad eam homini praestandam solae causae naturales, uti diximus, non sufficiebant; idcirco potius absolute supernaturalis dici debet immortalitas homini integro, quam naturalis. Unde propositio illa qua dicitur immortalitatem primi hominis non fuisse gratiae beneficium, sed naturalem conditionem, merito a sede Apostolica improbata est: maxime si sensus ejus sit immortalitatem ita esse debitam naturae humanae, ut Deus non potuerit eam creare mortalem. Hoc enim constat esse falsissimum.
latin.1677: XIX. Quod spectat autem Scholae Reformatae Doctores, illi quoque communi consensu docent hominem in statu innocentiae fuisse aliquatenus immortalem. Nec etiam dissimili ratione explicant istam immortalitatem. Nam cum Doctoribus Ecclesiae Romanae, distinguunt inter immortalitatem qua aliquis non potest mori, & inter eam qua aliquis potest non mori, & est a necessitate moriendi immunis. Priori modo solos beatos post resurrectionem immortales fore docent; sed posteriori tantum hominem in statu integro fuisse immortalem; ita ut in eo esset possibilitas moriendi, quae non est in beatis, non esset vero, quae jam est in nobis per peccatum, moriendi necessitas.
latin.1678: XX. Hanc rem sic exponit Josue Placeus Thesibus de statu Adami ante lapsum Thesi 32. Non erat, inquit, immortalis Adamus, quomodo nos erimus post beatam resurrectionem: poterat enim, ut peccare, sic mori. Nec erat mortalis, quemadmodum nos mortales sumus in hoc statu peccati: poterat enim, ut non peccare, ita non mori.
latin.1679: XXI. Et similiter Pareus immortalitatem illam, qua homo ante peccatum corpore immortalis erat, dicit fuisse potentiam non moriendi, seu negationem actus moriendi, ex hypothesi unionis cum anima originaliter perfecta, licet corpus hominis esset in se mortale. Immortalitas, inquit, significat primo impotentiam moriendi absolutam & natura. Sic solus Deus immortalitatem habet. Sic Patres negant, & nos negamus hominem immortalem fuisse natura. Secundo impotentiam moriendi ex gratia creationis: Sic Angeli, animae humanae sunt immortales. Tertio impotentiam moriendi ex gratia doni: sic corpora beatorum immortalitatem habebunt. Quarto potentiam non moriendi, seu negationem actus moriendi, ex aliqua hypothesi, licet in se sit mortale. Sic homo ante peccatum immortalis erat corpore, ex hypothesi unionis cum anima originaliter perfecta, immortali. In lib. adversus Bell. de Grat. primi hominis, cap. 9.
latin.1680: XXII. Tilenus quoque Disputatione de statu externo primi hominis thesi nona. Sciendum est, inquit, immortalitatem primi hominis non plane ejusdem fuisse rationis cum gloriosa Beatorum immortalitate. Nam ut aliud est posse non peccare, & non posse peccare: sic aliud posse non mori, & non posse mori. Illud est naturae, hoc gloriae. Prior immortalitas moriendi actum tollit, potestatem non excludit: posterior utrumque abolet & extinguit.
latin.1681: XXIII. Caeterum istam immortalitatem quae homini in integritate primigenia competebat, pertendunt dici debere potius naturalem quam supernaturalem, & revera primum hominem aliquo sensu fuisse natura immortalem. Haec est doctrina Tileni Disputationis modo citatae Thesi octava. Ubi asserit hominem vere dici natura immortalem. Thesi tamen secunda mentem suam distinctius explicans, docet corpus primi hominis per se quidem fuisse corruptibile, quippe ex contrariis, & inter se pugnantibus qualitatibus conflatum: Veruntamen ex Dei pacto incorruptibile fuisse futurum, si homo in Dei obsequio constitisset sine peccato.
latin.1682: XXIV. Sic etiam ea de re pronunciat Josue Placeus thesi jam allegata. Tam naturalis, inquit, erat Adamo facultas non moriendi, quam non peccandi. Haud magis est a natura mortis quam peccati imperium. Possibilitatem quidem moriendi a natura habuit, necessitatem vero a peccato. Cujus rei hanc rationem affert, quod aequum sit facultates Physicas sequi conditionem Moralium, penes quas est imperium in homine: Unde colligit in Adamo eandem fuisse rationem vitae & justitiae. Ac proinde cum justitia ipsi fuerit naturalis, naturalem quoque esse debuisse non moriendi facultatem.
latin.1683: XXV. Pareus vero distinguit inter naturam integram & naturam corruptam. Et dicit Adami immortalitatem, respectu naturae integrae fuisse naturalem: respectu vero naturae corruptae, non immortalitatem, sed mortalitatem, quae est moriendi necessitas, naturalem recte dici. Ac praeterea distinguit inter hominem integrum, & corpus ejus in se consideratum. Et homini, non corpori in se, immortalitatem naturalem fuisse asserit, in caput nonum Bellarmini de gratia primi hominis. Capite vero quinto homini integro docet naturale fuisse quicquid principiis naturae, ad ejus perfectionem per se adjacebat; & sine quo natura in suis principiis non erat primitus condita.
latin.1684: XXVI. Porro in hac quaestione illud omnino certum est, &, ut ex dictis apparet, communi consensu Scholae tam Romanae quam Reformatae probatum, hominem ante peccatum fuisse a necessitate moriendi immunem, in eo tamen fuisse, ut peccandi, sic etiam moriendi possibilitatem. Et hominem non alio quam isto sensu fuisse immortalem.
latin.1685: XXVII. Nec etiam negant Scholae Romanae Theologi, ut supra fuit a nobis ostensum, immortalitatem istam, quae primo homini ante peccatum competebat, naturalem certo respectu & sensu dici posse, nempe quatenus naturale significat quod est a prima Origine insitum, non autem adventitium atque superadditum: Item quatenus naturale opponitur ei quod est contra naturam, & significat id quod eandem naturam ornat atque perficit.
latin.1686: XXVIII. Quaestio solum remanet An simpliciter loquendo immortalitas ista dici potius debeat naturalis quam supernaturalis Respectu hominis integri? Quod affirmant Protestantes, Doctores vero Scholae Romanae negant.
latin.1687: XXIX. Verum quaestio ista solum est de nomine, respectu eorum qui inter Protestantes naturale cum Paraeo definiunt, Id sine quo natura in suis principiis non fuit primitus condita. Hoc enim sensu fatentur, ut vidimus, Doctores Scholae Romanae immortalitatem fuisse primo homini naturalem.
latin.1688: XXX. Dissidium solum quoddam reale remanebit inter eos ex Protestantibus qui volunt, sine omni auxilio supernaturali, hominem integrum mortem in perpetuum potuisse vitare, & Scholam Romanam quae id communi consensu negat.
latin.1689: XXXI. Caeterum modo constet necessitatem moriendi quae jam nobis incumbit non a natura, sed a peccato esse; & si homo in primaeva integritate perstitisset, vitam cum ejus justitia semper fuisse conjungendam, ex sapientissimo & aequissimo Dei instituto, quaestio ista non videtur ita magni esse momenti.
latin.1690: XXXII. Ut distinctius tamen aperiam quis sit meus ea de re sensus. Observo in Scholis Reformatis, circa perpetuo futuram hominis integri vitam, duas esse sententias. Etenim nonnulli sunt qui censent primum hominem, si juxta naturae foedus cum ipso a Deo contractum, in obsequio Dei permansisset, perpetuo quidem victurum fuisse, sed solummodo vita terrena atque animali, quae in caelestem atque gloriosam nunquam commutanda fuisset. Quae est doctrina Mosis Amyraldi Thesibus de tribus foederibus divinis.
latin.1691: XXXIII. Communior vero sententia tenet, hominem si primigenia integritate nunquam excidisset, assumendum tandem fuisse ad beatam & gloriosam in caelis immortalitatem, post decursum aliquod in his terris spatium, prout sapientiae divinae visum esset. Idque per immutationem similem illi quam experientur pii & sancti homines, quos ultimum judicium in terra vivos deprehendet.
latin.1692: XXXIV. Si hanc, quae communior & probabilior est, sententiam sequamur, certum est hominem nunquam perpetuo victurum fuisse absque auxilio supernaturali. Nam immutatio illa per quam homo fuisset in vitam caelestem assumptus, non fuisset naturalis, sed supernaturalis.
latin.1693: XXXV. Hominem autem in aeternum vivere potuisse vita terrena atque animali, ut prior illa sententia asserit, absque ullo supernaturali dono, vel auxilio, nullo modo mihi probabile videtur. Nec enim capere possum quomodo corpus ex elementis constans, adeoque naturaliter & in se corruptibile, absque ullo supra naturam auxilio, a corruptione possit in perpetuum praeservari. Qua in re judicium sequor Petri Molinaei, cui quoque dubium non est quin, homo quantumvis perfecto corporis temperamento naturali, opus habeat auxilio supernaturali, & Dei ope continua ad servandam hanc εὐκρασίαν. De statu Innocentiae Thesi 50.

sections.title: Estius' answer: Adam's immortality was in one way natural, in another above nature
sections.pass_a: But so that it may be understood more distinctly what is the opinion of the Doctors of the Roman School on this question, it seemed good to report here what William Estius very accurately and clearly teaches on the matter on the second book of the Sentences, Distinction 19, number 9. For there to the question, Whether the immortality of the first state was natural to man, he Responds by many and various distinctions. And he teaches that it was to him in a certain respect natural, and in a certain respect above nature; just as death too for fallen man is in a certain respect natural, in a certain respect against nature.
pass_b: To make the view of the Roman school's teachers on this question clearer, I think it worth setting out what William Estius teaches on it, very precisely and clearly, in his commentary on the second book of the Sentences, distinction 19, number 9.

There he answers the question "Whether the immortality of the first state was natural to man" with many different distinctions. He teaches that it was natural to man in one respect and above nature in another, just as death is natural to fallen man in one respect and against nature in another.

lemmas.gloss: I think it worth setting out here

choices.why: Estius keeps 'supra naturam' distinct from 'contra naturam'; the English keeps both prepositions.

sections.title: First sense: natural as belonging to nature's first institution
sections.pass_a: For first that is called natural which is present from the first institution of nature. And in this respect he says that immortality was natural to the first man, but death against nature, since man was instituted at the beginning immortal, that is, free from the necessity of dying.
pass_b: First, what is present from nature's first institution is called natural. In this sense he says that immortality was natural to the first man and death against nature, since man was created immortal at the beginning, that is, free from the necessity of dying.

lemmas.gloss: free from the necessity of dying

choices.why: Institutio here is God's first making of man; 'created' keeps the sense without the legal tone of 'instituted'.

sections.title: Second sense: natural as what every appetite seeks
sections.pass_a: Likewise that is called natural toward which the appetite of each thing is naturally borne. And in this way too he concedes that immortality is natural to man, and death against nature, since all by nature desire immortality, but flee death.
pass_b: Again, what each thing's appetite naturally tends toward is called natural. In this sense too he grants that immortality is natural to man and death against nature, because everyone by nature longs for immortality and shrinks from death.

choices.why: Estius concedes the point within one sense only; 'grants' keeps that limited concession.

sections.title: Third sense: natural as what one has from birth, whether good or not
sections.pass_a: Further, natural can signify what is in each one from birth, whether it be good and fitting to nature, and agreeable to natural appetite, or not. And thus too he confesses that immortality was natural to the first man, but mortality to us. For he was created immortal, but we are born liable to death.
pass_b: Natural can also mean what each person has from birth, whether it is good for nature, suited to it and in keeping with natural appetite, or not. In this sense too, he admits, immortality was natural to the first man and mortality is natural to us. He was created immortal; we are born subject to death.

choices.why: The point is that birth-natural need not be good; the English keeps the either-or in the Latin order.

sections.title: Fourth sense: natural as having its cause in nature; the body's temperament and the tree of life
sections.pass_a: Again he adds that that is called natural which has its cause in nature itself. And also, he says, in this manner immortality was to the first man in a certain way natural. For immortality consisted in the best temperament of the human body as an internal cause, and in the tree of life as an external cause (each of which was natural toward that effect).
pass_b: He adds that what has its cause in nature itself is called natural. "In this way too," he says, "immortality was in a manner natural to the first man. For it rested on the excellent balance of the human body as its inner cause and on the tree of life as its outer cause, and each of these was a natural cause of that effect."

lemmas.gloss: the excellent balance (temperament) of the human body

choices.why: Estius hedges with quodammodo; the English keeps the hedge.

notes: The tree of life is that of Genesis 2:9; the print gives no reference.

sections.title: Yet Estius calls it simply supernatural: from original righteousness and the earthy body; Baius rightly condemned
sections.pass_a: But he teaches that in another respect the same immortality was supernatural to man: partly indeed by reason of justice, on which that good constitution of the body, and consequently immortality itself, depended. For that justice, he says, was supernatural, inasmuch as through it the soul was subjected to God, and adhered to him, as to its supernatural good and end. While that subjection lasted, there was in the soul a certain supernatural force, through which it could preserve the body from all corruption. Partly by reason of the body, or the matter from which man was made. Which since it was earthly, did not have in itself the cause of immortality, but rather of mortality. Although therefore, he says, the first man had in nature itself some cause of immortality, yet not full and total. Nay rather if we separate in thought supernatural gifts from him, and consider in him only the natural things, he was mortal, so that it was necessary that he die. For he was composed of contraries, upon whose conflict there necessarily follows at last the corruption of the composite itself. According to this mode therefore immortality was supernatural to the first man. But since supernatural is properly opposed not to what is called natural in the first, second, or third mode of the modes already enumerated, but only to that in the fourth mode: according to which however immortality cannot be called simply natural to the first man; because to furnish it to man natural causes alone, as we said, did not suffice; therefore the immortality of integral man ought to be called absolutely supernatural rather than natural. Whence that proposition by which it is said that the immortality of the first man was not a benefit of grace, but a natural condition, was deservedly disapproved by the Apostolic see: especially if its sense is that immortality was so owed to human nature, that God could not create it mortal. For this is established to be most false.
pass_b: But Estius teaches that in another respect this same immortality was supernatural to man. Partly because of righteousness, on which the body's good constitution, and so immortality itself, depended. "That righteousness," he says, "was supernatural, inasmuch as through it the soul was subject to God and clung to him as its supernatural good and end. As long as that subjection lasted, the soul had a certain supernatural power by which it could keep the body from all corruption." And partly because of the body, that is, the matter from which man was made. Since that matter was earthy, it held in itself no cause of immortality, but rather of mortality.

"So although the first man," he says, "had in his very nature some cause of immortality, it was not a full and complete one. On the contrary, if in thought we set his supernatural gifts aside and consider only what was natural in him, he was mortal, so that he would have had to die. For he was made of contraries, and the dissolution of the compound necessarily follows from their conflict in the end. In this way, then, immortality was supernatural to the first man.

"But the supernatural is properly opposed not to what is called natural in the first, second or third of the senses just listed, but only to what is natural in the fourth sense. In that sense the first man's immortality cannot be called simply natural, because, as we said, natural causes alone were not enough to give it to him. So the immortality of unfallen man should be called supernatural, absolutely speaking, rather than natural.

"That is why the Apostolic See rightly condemned the proposition that the first man's immortality was not a gift of grace but a natural condition, especially if it means that immortality was so owed to human nature that God could not have created it mortal. That is clearly utterly false."

choices.why: Estius' conclusion is about the simple (unqualified) predicate, after granting qualified senses of 'natural'.
rejected: entirely beyond nature in every sense

notes: The condemned proposition is the Baius article cited in thesis XII.

sections.title: The Reformed agree: unfallen man could not-die, but only the risen blessed cannot die
sections.pass_a: But as regards the Doctors of the Reformed School, they too by common consent teach that man in the state of innocence was to some extent immortal. Nor do they explain that immortality in a dissimilar way. For with the Doctors of the Roman Church they distinguish between the immortality by which someone cannot die, and that by which someone can not-die, and is immune from the necessity of dying. They teach that in the former way only the blessed after the resurrection will be immortal; but that man in the integral state was immortal only in the latter; so that in him there was the possibility of dying, which is not in the blessed, but there was not the necessity of dying, which is now in us through sin.
pass_b: As for the teachers of the Reformed school, they too hold by common consent that man in the state of innocence was immortal in some measure, and they explain that immortality in much the same way.

Like the teachers of the Roman Church, they distinguish the immortality by which someone is unable to die from the immortality by which someone is able not to die and is free from the necessity of dying. In the first sense, they teach, only the blessed after the resurrection will be immortal. Man in his unfallen state was immortal only in the second sense: he had the possibility of dying, which the blessed do not have, but not the necessity of dying, which we now have through sin.

choices.why: Litotes ('not unlike') rendered positively.

sections.title: Placaeus: Adam was neither immortal as the risen will be nor mortal as we are
sections.pass_a: Josué de la Place sets out this matter thus in the Theses on the state of Adam before the fall, Thesis 32. Adam, he says, was not immortal in the way that we shall be after the blessed resurrection: for he could, as sin, so die. Nor was he mortal, in the way that we are mortal in this state of sin: for he could, as not sin, so not die.
pass_b: Josué de la Place (Placaeus) puts it this way in thesis 32 of his Theses on the State of Adam before the Fall: "Adam's immortality was not the kind we shall have after the blessed resurrection, since he was able to sin and so able to die. Nor was his mortality the kind we have now in this state of sin, since he was able to avoid sin and so able to avoid death."

lemmas.gloss: as he could sin, so he could die

lemmas.latin: ut non peccare, ita non mori
lemmas.gloss: as he could not-sin, so he could not-die

choices.term: poterat enim, ut non peccare, ita non mori
choices.english: just as he could avoid sinning, so he could avoid dying
choices.why: Keeps the parallel posse non peccare / posse non mori that the thesis turns on.
rejected: he could not sin and could not die
he was unable to sin or die

notes: Josué de la Place (Placaeus) taught at Saumur; the theses cited are from the Saumur Theses theologicae.

sections.title: Pareus' four senses of immortality: unfallen Adam's was the power of not dying, given union with a perfect soul
sections.pass_a: And similarly Pareus says that that immortality, by which man before sin was immortal in body, was the power of not dying, or the negation of the act of dying, on the hypothesis of union with a soul originally perfect, although the body of man was in itself mortal. Immortality, he says, signifies first the impotence of dying absolute and by nature. So God alone has immortality. So the Fathers deny, and we deny, that man was immortal by nature. Second the impotence of dying from the grace of creation: So Angels, human souls are immortal. Third the impotence of dying from the grace of gift: so the bodies of the blessed will have immortality. Fourth the power of not dying, or the negation of the act of dying, from some hypothesis, although in itself it be mortal. So man before sin was immortal in body, on the hypothesis of union with an immortal soul originally perfect. In the book against Bellarmine on the Grace of the first man, chapter 9.
pass_b: Pareus likewise says that the immortality by which man before sin was immortal in body was a power of not dying, that is, the absence of the act of dying, on the supposition of its union with a soul perfect from its origin, although man's body was mortal in itself.

"Immortality," he says, "means first an inability to die that is absolute and by nature. In this sense God alone has immortality, and in this sense the Fathers deny, and we deny, that man was immortal by nature. Second, an inability to die by the grace of creation: so angels and human souls are immortal. Third, an inability to die by the grace of a gift: so the bodies of the blessed will have immortality. Fourth, a power of not dying, that is, the absence of the act of dying, on some supposition, though the thing is mortal in itself. In this sense man before sin was immortal in body, on the supposition of its union with an immortal soul perfect from its origin." (Pareus, against Bellarmine, On the Grace of the First Man, chapter 9.)

choices.english: the absence of the act of dying
choices.why: Scholastic 'negatio' is absence, not denial; the English avoids implying a refusal.

notes: 'God alone has immortality' echoes 1 Timothy 6:16; the print gives no reference.

sections.title: Tilenus: posse non mori is of nature, non posse mori of glory
sections.pass_a: Tilenus also in the Disputation on the external state of the first man, ninth thesis. It must be known, he says, that the immortality of the first man was not plainly of the same character as the glorious immortality of the Blessed. For as it is one thing to be able not to sin, and not to be able to sin: so it is one thing to be able not to die, and not to be able to die. That is of nature, this of glory. The former immortality takes away the act of dying, does not exclude the power: the latter abolishes and extinguishes both.
pass_b: Tilenus says the same in his Disputation on the External State of the First Man, ninth thesis: "It should be understood that the first man's immortality was not wholly of the same kind as the glorious immortality of the blessed. For as being able not to sin is one thing and being unable to sin another, so being able not to die is one thing and being unable to die another. The first belongs to nature, the second to glory. The first kind of immortality removes the act of dying but does not rule out the power to die; the second abolishes and extinguishes both."

lemmas.gloss: not wholly of the same kind

choices.english: The first belongs to nature, the second to glory
choices.why: Illud/hoc refer back to the two powers just named; the English makes the order explicit.

notes: Daniel Tilenus (1563-1633) taught at Sedan before Le Blanc.

sections.title: Tilenus holds this immortality natural rather than supernatural, yet by God's covenant, not the body's own power
sections.pass_a: But they contend that that immortality which belonged to man in his primeval integrity ought to be called natural rather than supernatural, and that in truth the first man was in some sense immortal by nature. This is the doctrine of Tilenus in the Disputation just cited, eighth Thesis. Where he asserts that man is truly called immortal by nature. Yet in the second Thesis explaining his mind more distinctly, he teaches that the body of the first man was indeed of itself corruptible, being compounded of contrary and mutually conflicting qualities: But that by God's covenant it would have been incorruptible, if man had stood in God's obedience without sin.
pass_b: The Reformed, however, maintain that the immortality man had in his first integrity should be called natural rather than supernatural, and that the first man really was in some sense immortal by nature. This is what Tilenus teaches in the eighth thesis of the disputation just cited, where he says that man is truly called immortal by nature.

Yet in the second thesis, explaining his meaning more precisely, he teaches that the first man's body was in itself corruptible, since it was made up of contrary qualities in conflict with one another, but that by God's covenant it would have been incorruptible had man continued in obedience to God without sin.

choices.why: The implied subject is the Reformed doctors of thesis XIX; the English names them so the turn from Rome is clear.

sections.title: Placaeus: the power of not dying was as natural to Adam as the power of not sinning
sections.pass_a: So also Josué de la Place pronounces on the matter in the thesis already cited. As natural, he says, was to Adam the faculty of not dying, as of not sinning. Not more is the dominion of death from nature than that of sin. The possibility indeed of dying he had from nature, but the necessity from sin. For which matter he brings this reason, that it is fair that the Physical faculties follow the condition of the Moral, with which lies the rule in man: Whence he gathers that in Adam the account of life and of justice was the same. And therefore since justice was natural to him, the faculty of not dying also ought to have been natural.
pass_b: Josué de la Place says the same in the thesis already cited: "The power of not dying was as natural to Adam as the power of not sinning. The reign of death is no more from nature than the reign of sin. He had the possibility of dying from nature, but the necessity of dying from sin."

He gives this reason: it is fitting that the physical powers follow the condition of the moral powers, which rule in man. From this he concludes that in Adam life and righteousness stood on the same footing, and so, since righteousness was natural to him, the power of not dying must have been natural too.

lemmas.latin: penes quas est imperium in homine

choices.term: Haud magis est a natura mortis quam peccati imperium
choices.english: The reign of death is no more from nature than the reign of sin
choices.why: Imperium governs both genitives; the English repeats 'reign' to keep the parallel.
rejected: Death is not natural, nor sin's rule
Death's power is less natural than sin's

notes: 'Reign of death ... reign of sin' echoes Romans 5:14 and 5:21; the print gives no reference.

sections.title: Pareus: natural to integral nature, and to the whole man, not to the body in itself
sections.pass_a: But Pareus distinguishes between integral nature and corrupt nature. And he says that Adam's immortality was natural in respect of integral nature: but in respect of corrupt nature, not immortality, but mortality, which is the necessity of dying, is rightly called natural. And moreover he distinguishes between integral man, and his body considered in itself. And he asserts that immortality was natural to the man, not to the body in itself, on the ninth chapter of Bellarmine on the grace of the first man. But in the fifth Chapter he teaches that natural to integral man was whatever belonged of itself to the principles of nature for its perfection; and without which nature in its principles was not first founded.
pass_b: Pareus distinguishes between nature unfallen and nature corrupted. He says that with respect to unfallen nature Adam's immortality was natural, but that with respect to corrupted nature it is not immortality but mortality, that is, the necessity of dying, that is rightly called natural.

He also distinguishes between unfallen man and man's body considered in itself, and holds that immortality was natural to the man, not to the body in itself (on Bellarmine, On the Grace of the First Man, chapter 9). In chapter 5 he teaches that whatever belonged of itself to the principles of nature for its perfection, and without which nature was not first made in its principles, was natural to unfallen man.

choices.english: to the man, not to the body in itself
choices.why: The whole contrast of the thesis rests on the person versus the body taken alone.

sections.title: Both schools agree: before sin man was free of the necessity of dying, yet able to sin and to die
sections.pass_a: Further, in this question this is wholly certain, and, as appears from what has been said, approved by the common consent of the School both Roman and Reformed, that man before sin was immune from the necessity of dying, yet was in this condition, that as of sinning, so also of dying he had the possibility. And that man was immortal in no other sense than that.
pass_b: In this question one thing is entirely certain and, as appears from what has been said, approved by the common consent of both the Roman and the Reformed schools: before sin man was free from the necessity of dying, yet so placed that he could sin, and so could also die. And man was immortal in no other sense than this.

choices.english: in no other sense than this
choices.why: Le Blanc's agreement is exclusive; the English keeps the restriction.

sections.title: Rome too allows this immortality natural in two senses: implanted from origin, and perfecting nature
sections.pass_a: Nor do the Theologians of the Roman School deny, as was shown by us above, that that immortality which belonged to the first man before sin can be called natural in a certain respect and sense, namely insofar as natural signifies what is implanted from the first Origin, not adventitious and superadded: Likewise insofar as natural is opposed to what is against nature, and signifies that which adorns and perfects that same nature.
pass_b: Nor do the theologians of the Roman school deny, as we showed above, that the immortality the first man had before sin can be called natural in a certain respect and sense. It can be so called insofar as "natural" means what was implanted from the first origin, not something added from outside and laid on top. It can also be so called insofar as "natural" is opposed to what is against nature and means what adorns and perfects that same nature.

lemmas.gloss: added from outside and laid on top

choices.english: in a certain respect and sense
choices.why: Keeps the restriction that Rome's concession is qualified.

sections.title: The only question left: is it, simply speaking, natural or supernatural?
sections.pass_a: The Question only remains Whether, speaking simply, that immortality ought rather to be called natural than supernatural In respect of integral man? Which the Protestants affirm, but the Doctors of the Roman School deny.
pass_b: The only question left is whether, simply speaking, this immortality should be called natural rather than supernatural with respect to unfallen man. The Protestants say yes; the teachers of the Roman school say no.

choices.english: The Protestants say yes; the teachers of the Roman school say no
choices.why: Plain affirm/deny keeps the two sides in Le Blanc's order.

sections.title: With Pareus' definition of natural, the dispute is only about a word
sections.pass_a: But that question is only about the name, in respect of those among the Protestants who define natural with Pareus, That without which nature in its principles was not first founded. For in this sense, as we have seen, the Doctors of the Roman School confess that immortality was natural to the first man.
pass_b: But for those Protestants who define "natural" with Pareus as "that without which nature was not first made in its principles," the question is only about a word. For in that sense, as we have seen, the teachers of the Roman school admit that immortality was natural to the first man.

choices.why: Le Blanc means a verbal, not real, disagreement; that contrast is picked up in the next thesis.
rejected: is about a name only, not a reality

notes: Pareus' definition is the one cited from his chapter 5 in thesis XXV.

sections.title: A real dispute remains only with Protestants who think unfallen man needed no supernatural help to escape death
sections.pass_a: Only a certain real disagreement will remain between those of the Protestants who hold that, without all supernatural aid, integral man could have avoided death forever, and the Roman School which by common consent denies that.
pass_b: The only real disagreement left will be between those Protestants who hold that unfallen man could have escaped death forever without any supernatural help, and the Roman school, which by common consent denies it.

choices.why: Contrasts with the verbal dispute of the previous thesis.

sections.title: So long as death is from sin and life was joined to righteousness by God's decree, the question matters little
sections.pass_a: But provided it be established that the necessity of dying which now lies upon us is not from nature, but from sin; and that if man had persisted in primeval integrity, life would always have been to be joined with his justice, by the most wise and most just ordinance of God, that question does not seem to be of so great moment.
pass_b: Still, provided it is agreed that the necessity of dying that now lies on us comes not from nature but from sin, and that had man persevered in his original integrity, life would always have been joined to his righteousness by God's most wise and most just decree, this question does not seem very important.

choices.term: non videtur ita magni esse momenti
choices.why: Le Blanc's irenic understatement; the English does not dismiss the question outright.

sections.title: Two Reformed views; Amyraut: unfallen man would have lived forever, but only an earthly life
sections.pass_a: But that I may open more distinctly what my opinion on the matter is. I observe in the Reformed Schools, concerning the life of integral man that would have been perpetual, that there are two opinions. For there are some who think that the first man, if according to the covenant of nature contracted with him by God he had remained in God's obedience, would indeed have lived perpetually, but only with an earthly and animal life, which would never have been changed into a heavenly and glorious one. Which is the doctrine of Moses Amyraut in the Theses on the three divine covenants.
pass_b: To make my own view on this clearer: I find two opinions in the Reformed schools about the unending life unfallen man would have had.

Some hold that if the first man had remained in obedience to God, according to the covenant of nature God made with him, he would indeed have lived forever, but only with an earthly, animal life that would never have been changed into a heavenly and glorious one. This is what Moses Amyraut teaches in his Theses on the Three Divine Covenants.

choices.why: Animalis is the Pauline 'natural / soulish' life (1 Corinthians 15:44-46), contrasted with heavenly; the English keeps Le Blanc's word.

notes: Moses Amyraut's Theses de tribus foederibus divinis were disputed at Saumur.

sections.title: The commoner view: after a span on earth man would have been changed into heavenly glory
sections.pass_a: But the more common opinion holds that man, if he had never fallen from primeval integrity, would at last have been taken up to blessed and glorious immortality in the heavens, after some course of time on these lands, as it would have seemed good to divine wisdom. And that through a change similar to that which pious and holy men will experience, whom the last judgment will find alive on earth.
pass_b: The more common opinion holds that if man had never fallen from his original integrity, he would at last have been taken up into a blessed and glorious immortality in heaven, after spending some span of time on this earth, as God's wisdom saw fit.
This would have happened through a change like the one the godly and holy will undergo who are found alive on earth at the last judgment.

choices.term: quos ultimum judicium in terra vivos deprehendet
choices.english: who are found alive on earth at the last judgment
choices.why: Deprehendet keeps the judgment as the one that finds them; the English keeps the living saints as the subject of the change.

notes: The change of the living echoes 1 Corinthians 15:51-52 and 1 Thessalonians 4:17; the print gives no reference.

sections.title: On that view man would never have lived forever without supernatural help
sections.pass_a: If we follow this opinion, which is more common and more probable, it is certain that man would never have lived perpetually without supernatural aid. For that change through which man would have been taken up into heavenly life would not have been natural, but supernatural.
pass_b: This opinion is both the more common and the more probable. On it, plainly, man could never have gone on living forever unless God helped him beyond nature, since the change that was to carry him up into heavenly life would itself have been a supernatural change, not a natural one.

choices.english: would have been not natural but supernatural
choices.why: Keeps the closing antithesis on which Le Blanc's view turns.

sections.title: Le Blanc: an endless earthly life without supernatural help is improbable; he follows Pierre du Moulin. De Primi Hominis Immortalitate closes
sections.pass_a: But that man could have lived eternally with an earthly and animal life, as that former opinion asserts, without any supernatural gift, or aid, seems to me in no way probable. For I cannot grasp how a body consisting of elements, and so naturally and in itself corruptible, could be preserved forever from corruption without any aid above nature. In which matter I follow the judgment of Pierre du Moulin, to whom also there is no doubt that man, however perfect the natural temperament of his body, has need of supernatural aid, and of God's continual help to preserve this eukrasia. On the state of Innocence, Thesis 50.
pass_b: But that man could have lived forever an earthly, animal life without any supernatural gift or help, as the first opinion maintains, seems to me in no way probable. I cannot see how a body made of the elements, and so naturally and in itself corruptible, could be kept from corruption forever without some help above nature.

Here I follow the judgment of Pierre du Moulin, who also has no doubt that man, however perfect the natural balance of his body, needs supernatural help and God's continual aid to keep that good balance (eukrasia) (Du Moulin, On the State of Innocence, thesis 50).

choices.why: Temperamentum is the humoral blend; 'balance' carries it into plain English and links it to eukrasia.

notes: Pierre du Moulin (Molinaeus) taught at Sedan; the theses cited are his disputations on the state of innocence.
